core: Trauma-informed care as a framework for how services are organized and delivered, explicitly distinct from trauma treatment
SAMHSA's 2014 concept of trauma: the three E's - event(s), the individual's experience of them, and lasting adverse effects
The four R's: realize, recognize, respond, and actively resist re-traumatization
The six key principles: safety; trustworthiness and transparency; peer support; collaboration and mutuality; empowerment, voice and choice; cultural, historical and gender issues
The ten implementation domains, and the requirement that the approach be built into policy rather than left to training days and individual goodwill

Re-traumatization produced by ordinary agency practice: intake questioning, physical environment, waiting, unexplained rules and power differentials, restraint and seclusion, staff turnover and referral hand-offs
Universal precautions: designing services on the assumption that trauma histories are present rather than screening to find out who has one
The reframing from 'what is wrong with you' to 'what happened to you', attributed to Foderaro as quoted in Bloom (1995) and reported in Sweeney and colleagues (2018)
The state of the evidence for trauma-informed organizational interventions, per the AHRQ 2025 systematic review
Why using an ACE score to make decisions about an individual is a misuse of ACE research
supporting: Prevalence figures that motivate a universal-precautions design (National Comorbidity Survey figures as reported in SAMHSA TIP 57; CDC's ACE prevalence estimates)
The parallel process: staff safety, trust and voice as part of the same framework
Peer support as a named principle, and the SAMHSA position that everyone in an organization has a role
Relationship to strengths-based practice and the person-in-environment perspective (referenced, not re-taught)

The biology of the stress response, PTSD as a diagnosis, resilience research, and secondary traumatic stress - owned by stress-trauma-and-resilience
Trauma-specific treatments (EMDR, TF-CBT, prolonged exposure) beyond naming that they are a different category of thing

Individualized clinical, diagnostic, treatment, legal or benefits advice

claims.claim: SAMHSA's 2014 guidance defines individual trauma as resulting from an event, series of events, or set of circumstances experienced by the individual as physically or emotionally harmful or life threatening, with lasting adverse effects on functioning and on mental, physical, social, emotional or spiritual well-being - the three E's of event, experience and effect.

The same event can be traumatic for one person and not for another; how it is experienced is shaped by cultural beliefs, available social support and developmental stage, and the adverse effects can be immediate or delayed, short or long term, and may not be connected by the person to the original events.

SAMHSA states a trauma-informed program, organization or system as four assumptions - it realizes the widespread impact of trauma and understands potential paths for recovery, recognizes signs and symptoms in clients, families, staff and others involved with the system, responds by fully integrating knowledge about trauma into policies, procedures and practices, and seeks to actively resist re-traumatization.

SAMHSA names six key principles of a trauma-informed approach - safety; trustworthiness and transparency; peer support; collaboration and mutuality; empowerment, voice and choice; and cultural, historical and gender issues - and presents them as principles rather than a prescribed set of practices or procedures.

A trauma-informed approach is distinct from trauma-specific services: it is inclusive of trauma-specific interventions such as assessment, treatment and recovery supports, but it works by incorporating trauma principles into the organizational culture, and it is therefore not itself a treatment.

SAMHSA describes the organizational response as a universal precautions approach in which the presence of trauma in the lives of the people served is expected and care is taken not to replicate it; SAMHSA TIP 57 adds that being trauma aware does not require assuming that every client has a trauma history, but anticipating the possibility from first contact, intake and screening onward.

SAMHSA gives restraint of a person who has been sexually abused and placement of a neglected and abandoned child in a seclusion room as examples of organizational practices that may re-traumatize; TIP 57 adds that standard or unexamined policies and practices can re-traumatize, that trauma-informed care begins at first contact, and that it requires everyone from receptionists and intake staff to supervisors, administrators and board members.

SAMHSA sets out ten implementation domains - governance and leadership; policy; physical environment; engagement and involvement; cross-sector collaboration; screening, assessment and treatment services; training and workforce development; progress monitoring and quality assurance; financing; and evaluation - and states that the approach must be hard-wired into practices and procedures rather than relying solely on training workshops or a well-intentioned leader.

The paradigm shift from asking 'what is wrong with you' to asking 'what happened to you' is attributed in the trauma-informed literature to Joseph Foderaro, quoted in Sandra Bloom's 1995 writing on creating sanctuary, and trauma-informed approaches are described as a process of organizational change rather than a service or a checklist of actions.

The original ACE Study was a collaboration between Kaiser Permanente's Health Appraisal Center in San Diego and the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention; the first report mailed a questionnaire to 13,494 adults who had completed a standardized medical evaluation at a large HMO and analyzed 9,508 responses (70.5 percent), and the full study population of 17,337 adult HMO members was roughly three-quarters white (73 percent of women, 76 percent of men) with 34 percent of women and 45 percent of men college graduates plus a further 37 percent and 34 percent with some college.

The ACE Study found a graded relationship between the number of categories of adverse childhood experience reported and multiple adult health risk behaviors and diseases - a population-level association.

Anda, Porter and Brown - two of them among the ACE Study's own investigators - published a 2020 commentary stating that the ACE score is a relatively crude measure of cumulative childhood stress exposure, that unlike blood pressure or lipid levels it has no measurement reference standards or cut points for clinical decision making, that they are concerned it is being misappropriated as a screening or diagnostic tool to infer individual risk and misapplied in treatment algorithms that assign population-based risk to individuals, and that programs promoting ACE screening should be evaluated against U.S. Preventive Services Task Force standards.

Baldwin and colleagues (2021) tested ACE screening in two birth cohorts (E-Risk, 2,009 analyzed; Dunedin, 918 analyzed) and found that ACE scores predicted mean group differences in later health but had poor accuracy for individuals - area under the curve 0.58 for any mental health problem and 0.60 for any physical health problem, against 0.50 for chance - concluding that targeting interventions on the basis of ACE screening is likely to be ineffective at preventing poor health outcomes.

An AHRQ Evidence-based Practice Center systematic review published in January 2025 searched literature through 19 July 2024, screened 4,379 unique references, found 12 eligible intervention studies reported in 16 publications, judged all of them at high risk of bias, and concluded that the evidence was insufficient to determine the effects of trauma-informed care on client health-related outcomes in any setting or comparison; no included study collected information on harms or unintended consequences, and the review noted that trauma-informed care models vary considerably in their components.

A 2021 systematic review of 32 quantitative studies labeled trauma-informed found the label applied mostly to clinical treatments delivered by medical professionals in outpatient settings - eye movement desensitization and reprocessing and cognitive behavioral therapy were the two most frequent - and reported inconsistent evidence for psychological outcomes, with PTSD symptoms significantly reduced in 11 of 23 studies that measured them.

Trauma exposure is common enough in the general population to make a universal-precautions design reasonable: SAMHSA TIP 57 reports first National Comorbidity Survey figures of 61 percent of men and 51 percent of women experiencing at least one trauma in their lifetime, and the CDC's ACEs page reported that about 64 percent of U.S. adults said they had experienced at least one type of adverse childhood experience and 17.3 percent reported four or more.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether trauma-informed organizational approaches improve outcomes for the people served.
positions: Sweeney and colleagues (2018) describe an emerging evidence base and report that a small number of studies have found reductions in symptoms and in the use of seclusion and restraint, better coping, retention and shorter inpatient stays.
The AHRQ systematic review (January 2025) found only 12 eligible comparative studies, all at high risk of bias, and rated the evidence insufficient for every outcome, setting and comparison.

Han and colleagues (2021) reviewed 32 studies carrying the trauma-informed label and found inconsistent evidence for psychological outcomes, with most studies actually testing established psychotherapies rather than organizational change.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson reports the AHRQ finding as the current state of the evidence because it is the most recent, most systematic and most explicitly graded assessment, and treats claims of benefit as promising but unestablished. It also makes the AHRQ point that insufficient evidence is not evidence of no benefit, and the Han point that the label is applied to very different things, which is part of why the literature cannot be pooled.

positions: Felitti and colleagues (1998) established a strong graded association between counts of adverse childhood experiences and adult health risks at the population level.
Anda, Porter and Brown (2020), including two of the study's own investigators, warn that the ACE score has no clinical reference standards or cut points and is being misapplied to individuals.
Baldwin and colleagues (2021) show empirically that ACE scores have near-chance accuracy for predicting which individual will develop later health problems.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson keeps population inference and individual inference separate, states that the ACE score was never validated as an individual screening or predictive instrument, and places the misuse in Common Mistakes as required. It reports the original cohort's composition (largely white, insured, mostly with at least some college) so students can see the generalization problem as well as the level-of-analysis problem.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft asserted nothing verifiable about trauma-informed care at all: it described the topic as 'a foundational concept in Social Work & Human Services' and offered a toolbox-drawer analogy and a map-legend analogy with no content.
The draft's vocabulary list defined the topic term as 'a foundational Social Work & Human Services concept covered in this lesson', which is circular and carries no information.
The draft implied the topic is a concept to apply to a scenario rather than an organizational framework with a named source, four assumptions, six principles and a contested evidence base.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the entire draft with content anchored in SAMHSA's own 2014 guidance, verified against the publication itself rather than a secondhand list of principles.
Added the explicit statement that trauma-informed care is not a treatment and that a practitioner delivering it is not doing therapy.
Added the ACE-score misuse to Common Mistakes with the original cohort's composition, the absence of clinical cut points, and the measured individual predictive accuracy.
Stated the actual state of the organizational evidence base with reference to the AHRQ 2025 review rather than asserting effectiveness.
Added an explicit educational-material statement and removed anything that could read as a screening protocol or clinical instruction.
rightsIssues: SAMHSA's 2014 guidance and TIP 57 are U.S. government publications carrying explicit public domain notices; even so, the lesson states the principles and assumptions in original wording rather than reproducing SAMHSA's text, apart from the six principle names, which are proper names of the principles and cannot be usefully renamed.

The AHRQ Bookshelf edition states that the publication is in the public domain while also stating that specific written permission is needed for commercial use; the source is therefore recorded as REFERENCE_ONLY and only its findings are reported.
Sweeney and colleagues (2018) is CC BY-NC-ND, which permits no derivatives; it is used as reference only and no wording is adapted.
Baldwin and colleagues (2021) and Han and colleagues (2021) are CC BY; both are cited by name in the lesson.

Felitti (1998), Anda (2006) and Anda (2020) are publisher-controlled; facts only, no wording reproduced. The Anda 2020 abstract was read from the publisher's abstract record because the full text was paywalled to this session.
The CDC page carries no stated reuse license and none is inferred from the .gov domain; it is recorded as REFERENCE_ONLY.

sourceRecords.title: SAMHSA's Concept of Trauma and Guidance for a Trauma-Informed Approach (HHS Publication No. (SMA) 14-4884)
sourceRecords.provider: Trauma and Justice Strategic Initiative, Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services
sourceRecords.license: Public domain notice printed in the publication: all materials except those taken directly from copyrighted sources may be reproduced or copied without permission; citation appreciated; not to be reproduced or distributed for a fee without written SAMHSA authorization.
sourceRecords.notes: The primary source for this lesson, read in full as a PDF (27 pages). Supports the working definition of individual trauma, the three E's, the four R's, the six key principles and their descriptions, the statement that a trauma-informed approach is distinct from trauma-specific services, the universal precautions formulation, the restraint and seclusion examples of re-traumatization, the ten implementation domains and the warning that the approach must be hard-wired rather than left to training workshops or a well-intentioned leader. Publication data verified from the document itself: prepared by SAMHSA's Trauma and Justice Strategic Initiative under the leadership of Larke N. Huang, July 2014, HHS Publication No. (SMA) 14-4884. SAMHSA's own store and library URLs did not resolve to the file during this research session, so the official PDF was read from an Internet Archive capture of store.samhsa.gov dated 2 January 2019; the archive's copy carries the same content digest as captures of the SAMHSA-hosted copy at ncsacw.samhsa.gov. Principle names are reproduced as proper names; no other wording is reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Trauma-Informed Care in Behavioral Health Services (Treatment Improvement Protocol Series No. 57, HHS Publication No. (SMA) 14-4816)
sourceRecords.provider: Center for Substance Abuse Treatment, Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services; read on NCBI Bookshelf
sourceRecords.license: Bookshelf record states that the publication is in the public domain
sourceRecords.notes: Part 1, Chapter 1 read in full (NBK207195). Supports: trauma-informed care as an intervention and organizational approach beginning at first contact and requiring every role from receptionists to board members; the statement that organizations and providers can re-traumatize clients through standard or unexamined policies and practices; the point that trauma awareness does not require assuming everyone has a trauma history but anticipating the possibility; the all-male group referral as a worked illustration of avoidable re-traumatization; and the National Comorbidity Survey prevalence figures of 61 percent of men and 51 percent of women reporting at least one lifetime trauma, which TIP 57 attributes to Kessler and colleagues (1999). Facts synthesized; wording not reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Trauma Informed Care: A Systematic Review (AHRQ Publication No. 25-EHC007)
sourceRecords.provider: Minnesota Evidence-based Practice Center for the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services; read on NCBI Bookshelf
sourceRecords.license: Bookshelf record states the publication is in the public domain; AHRQ's own notice on the same page states that specific written permission is needed for commercial use or use outside the United States
sourceRecords.notes: Structured abstract and front matter read. The single most important source for the lesson's evidence claim: searches through 19 July 2024, 4,379 unique references screened, 12 eligible studies in 16 publications across adult medical care, adult mental health, primary prevention for children, adolescent medical care and residential and non-residential child welfare; all studies high risk of bias; evidence insufficient for every outcome and comparison; no harms data collected; models vary considerably in components. The review's own caution - that insufficient evidence does not mean the interventions are useless - is reported in the lesson. Because the page carries two different statements about reuse, the record is conservative: findings reported, no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Trauma informed interventions: A systematic review (PLoS ONE 16(6): e0252747)
sourceRecords.provider: Han HR, Miller HN, Nkimbeng M, Budhathoki C, Mikhael T, Rivers E, Gray J, Trimble K, Chow S, Wilson P; Public Library of Science
sourceRecords.notes: Abstract verified through the Europe PMC record (PMC8219147). Supports the point that the trauma-informed label is applied inconsistently: of 32 studies, most tested established psychotherapies delivered by medical professionals in outpatient settings, with EMDR and CBT the most common, and the authors concluded that evidence for psychological outcomes is inconsistent. Used to explain why systematic reviews of this field cannot pool their results.

sourceRecords.title: A paradigm shift: relationships in trauma-informed mental health services (BJPsych Advances 24(5), 319-333)
sourceRecords.provider: Sweeney A, Filson B, Kennedy A, Collinson L, Gillard S; Royal College of Psychiatrists / Cambridge University Press
sourceRecords.notes: Full text read via Europe PMC (PMC6088388). Used for one thing the U.S. federal sources do not supply: the attribution of the 'what is wrong with you' to 'what happened to you' reframing to Foderaro, cited in Bloom (1995), 'Creating sanctuary in the school', Journal for a Just and Caring Education 1:403-33. Also supports the framing of trauma-informed approaches as a process of organizational change rather than a service or a checklist of actions, and the authors' own description of the evidence base as emerging. No derivatives permitted under the licence, so nothing is adapted and no wording is reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Relationship of childhood abuse and household dysfunction to many of the leading causes of death in adults: the Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACE) Study (American Journal of Preventive Medicine 14(4), 245-258)
sourceRecords.provider: Felitti VJ, Anda RF, Nordenberg D, Williamson DF, Spitz AM, Edwards V, Koss MP, Marks JS; Elsevier
sourceRecords.notes: Abstract verified through the Europe PMC record (PMID 9635069). Supports the original study design: a questionnaire mailed to 13,494 adults who had completed a standardized medical evaluation at a large HMO, 9,508 responses (70.5 percent), seven categories of adverse childhood experience, and a graded population-level relationship between the number of categories and adult health risk behaviors and diseases. Used for the population-level finding only; the lesson does not restate its effect sizes.

sourceRecords.title: The enduring effects of abuse and related adverse experiences in childhood: a convergence of evidence from neurobiology and epidemiology (European Archives of Psychiatry and Clinical Neuroscience 256(3), 174-186)
sourceRecords.provider: Anda RF, Felitti VJ, Bremner JD, Walker JD, Whitfield C, Perry BD, Dube SR, Giles WH; Springer, author manuscript on PubMed Central
sourceRecords.notes: Read on PubMed Central for the study-population facts the 1998 abstract does not carry: the ACE Study is a collaboration between Kaiser Permanente's Health Appraisal Center in San Diego and the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention; the full sample was 17,337 adult HMO members (9,367 women, 7,970 men; mean age 56 and 58); 73 percent of women and 76 percent of men were white; 34 percent of women and 45 percent of men were college graduates and a further 37 percent and 34 percent had some college. These figures support the lesson's statement that the founding cohort was largely white, insured and comparatively well educated. Article is not open access; facts only.

sourceRecords.title: Inside the Adverse Childhood Experience Score: Strengths, Limitations, and Misapplications (American Journal of Preventive Medicine 59(2), 293-295)
sourceRecords.provider: Anda RF, Porter LE, Brown DW; Elsevier
sourceRecords.license: Publisher records the article as hybrid open access under CC BY-NC-ND
sourceRecords.notes: The publisher's full text was blocked to this session, and the PubMed record carries no abstract; the abstract was read from the publisher's abstract record retrieved through the Semantic Scholar API, and the citation was confirmed against PubMed (PMID 32222260). Supports: the ACE score is a relatively crude measure of cumulative childhood stress exposure that varies widely between people; unlike blood pressure or lipid levels it has no measurement reference standards or cut points for clinical decision making; the authors' concern that ACE scores are being misappropriated as a screening or diagnostic tool to infer individual risk and misapplied in treatment algorithms that assign population-based risk to individuals; and their call for ACE screening programs to be evaluated against USPSTF standards. Anda is a founding ACE Study investigator, which is why this commentary carries weight. Because only the abstract was accessible, the lesson attributes to this source only what the abstract states.

sourceRecords.title: Population vs Individual Prediction of Poor Health From Results of Adverse Childhood Experiences Screening (JAMA Pediatrics 175(4), 385-393)
sourceRecords.provider: Baldwin JR, Caspi A, Meehan AJ, Ambler A, Arseneault L, Fisher HL, Harrington H, Matthews T, Odgers CL, Poulton R, Ramrakha S, Moffitt TE, Danese A; American Medical Association
sourceRecords.notes: Full text read on PubMed Central (PMC7835926). Supports the quantitative core of the ACE-misuse correction: in the E-Risk cohort (2,009 analyzed, followed to age 18) and the Dunedin cohort (918 analyzed, followed to age 45), ACE scores predicted mean group differences in health (relative risk 1.14 per additional ACE for any mental health problem, 1.09 for any physical health problem) but had poor individual accuracy, with areas under the curve of 0.58 and 0.60 against 0.50 for chance; the authors conclude that targeting interventions on the basis of ACE screening is likely to be ineffective at preventing poor health outcomes. Findings reported in the lesson's own wording.

sourceRecords.title: About Adverse Childhood Experiences
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sourceRecords.notes: Used only for prevalence context supporting the universal-precautions design argument: about 64 percent of U.S. adults reported at least one type of adverse childhood experience before age 18 and 17.3 percent reported four or more types. The page was blocked to direct retrieval from this session, so it was read from an Internet Archive capture dated 20 May 2024 of a page carrying a CDC review date of 9 April 2024; the lesson dates the figures accordingly and does not present them as current-year statistics. No reuse licence is stated on the page and none is inferred from the .gov domain. Note that this CDC page describes ACEs, prevalence, outcomes and prevention; it was not found to contain a statement about the use of ACE scores to screen individuals, so the lesson attributes that caution to Anda, Porter and Brown (2020) and to Baldwin and colleagues (2021) rather than to CDC.
